summary: Bleomycin is a cytotoxic glycopeptide antibiotic that causes DNA strand breaks and cell-cycle arrest, used as palliative chemotherapy for squamous cell carcinomas, Hodgkin and non-Hodgkin lymphoma, testicular germ cell tumors, and as a sclerosing agent for malignant pleural effusion. Its defining and most severe toxicity is dose-related pulmonary fibrosis (more common over a 400-unit total dose and in older patients), and a severe idiosyncratic reaction (hypotension, fever, chills, wheezing, confusion) occurs in about 1% of lymphoma patients - so first doses in lymphoma should be small test doses.
indications: Squamous cell carcinoma (head and neck, cervix, vulva, penis, skin, larynx) as palliative treatment
Hodgkin's disease and non-Hodgkin's lymphoma (e.g. ABVD regimen)
Testicular carcinoma - embryonal cell, choriocarcinoma, teratocarcinoma (e.g. BEP regimen)
Malignant pleural effusion - intrapleural sclerosing agent to prevent recurrence

moa: Bleomycin's main action is inhibition of DNA synthesis, with lesser effects on RNA and protein synthesis. It binds DNA and, in the presence of oxygen and metal ions (iron), generates free radicals that produce single- and double-strand DNA breaks, causing cell-cycle arrest in G2 and mitosis. Lack of the inactivating enzyme bleomycin hydrolase in skin and lung accounts for its characteristic cutaneous and pulmonary toxicity. Intrapleurally it acts as a chemical sclerosing agent.

absolute: Prior hypersensitive or idiosyncratic reaction to bleomycin
relative: Significant pre-existing pulmonary disease or reduced pulmonary reserve
Cumulative dose approaching or exceeding 400 units
monitor: Prior or concurrent thoracic radiotherapy (additive lung toxicity)
Concurrent oxygen therapy / high FiO2 during anesthesia
Concurrent cisplatin or nephrotoxins (reduced bleomycin clearance)
Concurrent G-CSF / cytokines (possible increased pulmonary toxicity)

preg: Pregnancy Category D - bleomycin can cause fetal harm when administered to a pregnant woman (teratogenic and embryotoxic in animals). Avoid in pregnancy; advise women of childbearing potential to use effective contraception and inform them of the potential hazard to the fetus.
lact: It is not known whether bleomycin is excreted in human milk. Because of the potential for serious adverse reactions in nursing infants, breastfeeding should be discontinued during bleomycin therapy.
renal: Bleomycin is eliminated predominantly by renal excretion; impaired renal function reduces clearance, prolongs half-life and increases toxicity. Reduce the dose in renal impairment and avoid nephrotoxic combinations; fatal pulmonary toxicity has occurred with unrecognized cisplatin-induced renal failure.
hepatic: Hepatic toxicity (deterioration of liver function tests) has been reported and may occur at any time during therapy. Use with caution and monitor liver function.

major: Nephrotoxic drugs, especially cisplatin - reduce bleomycin renal clearance, raising levels and pulmonary toxicity risk
Oxygen / high inspired oxygen concentration (e.g. during surgery) - potentiates pulmonary toxicity; keep FiO2 as low as feasible
moderate: G-CSF (filgrastim) and other cytokines - some reports of increased pulmonary toxicity (data conflicting)
Other antineoplastics - additive myelosuppression and toxicity per regimen
Anesthetic agents requiring high FiO2 - lung injury risk
minor: Live vaccines - avoid in immunosuppressed patients
Phenytoin/digoxin - reduced absorption reported with some cytotoxics
interactions.food: Parenteral administration; food interactions not applicable.
interactions.alcohol: Not directly relevant; avoid additional hepatotoxic exposures.
interactions.diagnostics: Monitor chest radiographs/CT, pulmonary function tests (especially DLCO), renal and hepatic function.

common: Fever and chills (often within hours of dosing)
Skin changes - erythema, hyperpigmentation, hyperkeratosis, striae, nail changes
serious: Pulmonary toxicity - pneumonitis progressing to pulmonary fibrosis (~10% incidence, ~1% fatal)
Idiosyncratic anaphylactoid reaction (hypotension, confusion, fever, chills, wheezing) in ~1% of lymphoma patients

monitoring: Pulmonary status - symptoms (dyspnea, fine basal rales), chest imaging and pulmonary function tests (DLCO) before and during therapy
Cumulative lifetime dose (heightened fibrosis risk above ~400 units)
Renal function (creatinine) and hepatic function tests
Close observation after the first 1-2 lymphoma doses for idiosyncratic reaction
Temperature and signs of acute reaction during and after each dose
counsel: Report any new or worsening cough, shortness of breath or chest tightness immediately (lung toxicity)
Fever and chills can occur within hours of a dose; tell your team if severe
Avoid high-oxygen exposure and tell any anesthetist/surgeon you have received bleomycin
Use effective contraception; do not breastfeed during treatment
Skin darkening, rash, mouth sores and hair loss may occur and usually improve after therapy
pk: Hodgkin/testicular tumor response often within 2 weeks; squamous cell over 3 weeks
Peak plasma concentration 30-60 minutes after IM/SC; immediate after IV
Terminal half-life ~2-4 hours (prolonged in renal impairment, up to ~6 h)
Dosed weekly or twice weekly per regimen
Store refrigerated 2-8 C; reconstitute in 0.9% sodium chloride (NOT dextrose)
pearls: Boxed warning: pulmonary fibrosis is the most severe toxicity - higher risk over 400 units total dose and in elderly patients, but can occur at low doses
Boxed warning: severe idiosyncratic reaction (hypotension, confusion, fever, chills, wheezing) in ~1% of lymphoma patients - give the first 2 lymphoma doses as <=2-unit test doses
Bleomycin causes minimal myelosuppression, making it useful in multidrug regimens (ABVD, BEP)
Avoid high inspired oxygen (e.g. during surgery) in patients who have received bleomycin - it potentiates lung injury
Reconstitute only in saline; dextrose degrades it. Reduce dose in renal impairment and avoid concurrent nephrotoxins like cisplatin without monitoring
missed: Bleomycin is administered by a clinician on a scheduled basis; there is no patient self-administered missed dose. A delayed or missed clinic dose is rescheduled by the oncology team, who will recalculate timing and cumulative dose.
overdose: Acute reactions to overdose include hypotension, fever, rapid pulse and general shock-like symptoms; chronic/cumulative overdose increases the risk of pulmonary fibrosis. There is no specific antidote. Treatment is symptomatic and supportive - manage hypotension, fever and respiratory complications; bleomycin is not effectively dialyzable. Watch closely for delayed pulmonary toxicity.
